questions.stem: A 3-day-old term newborn is noted to have a yellowish discoloration of the face and trunk. He is feeding well, has passed meconium, and was discharged at 24 hours. Total serum bilirubin is 14 mg/dL at 72 hours of life. Which of the following is the most important next step in management?
options: Plot the bilirubin on the hour-specific nomogram and repeat the level within 24 hours
Reassure the parents and review at the routine 2-week visit
Begin phototherapy immediately regardless of the level
Order a direct Coombs test and stop breastfeeding
questions.explanation: Jaundice in the first week must be risk-stratified using the hour-specific bilirubin nomogram, since the same value is low risk at 96 hours but high risk at 36 hours. Repeat measurement within 24 hours is required for values in the intermediate or high-intermediate zone. Simple reassurance is unsafe because bilirubin can rise rapidly in the first days, while immediate phototherapy is reserved for levels above the age-specific treatment threshold.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is brought to the clinic because of a barking cough and a hoarse voice that started overnight. He has a low-grade fever and inspiratory stridor at rest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor in a toddler with a preceding coryzal illness is the classic picture of croup, which is caused by parainfluenza virus. Epiglottitis is the closest distractor but presents with high fever, drooling, muffled voice and a toxic child sitting forward, without a barking cough. Bronchiolitis produces wheeze and fine crackles rather than stridor, and foreign body aspiration usually has a sudden onset without fever.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is being reviewed in the well-baby clinic. Which of the following developmental milestones is most consistent with his age?
questions.explanation: Most infants can sit without support by 6 to 8 months, making this the appropriate milestone for a 6-month-old. Walking independently normally appears around 12 to 15 months, a pincer grasp around 9 to 12 months, and meaningful words around 12 months. The other options describe milestones that would be precocious at this age.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 2-day history of fever, sore throat and a fine red rash that started on the neck and spread to the trunk. Examination shows a strawberry tongue, tonsillar exudate and tender enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: The features describe streptococcal pharyngitis with a scarlatiniform rash, and penicillin V for a full 10-day course is the treatment of choice to eradicate the organism and prevent rheumatic fever. A 3-day course of amoxicillin is inadequate because full courses are needed to prevent suppurative and nonsuppurative complications. Azithromycin is reserved for penicillin allergy, and supportive care alone risks rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: A newborn delivered at 39 weeks is noted at 6 hours of life to have tachypnoea, grunting and nasal flaring. Chest radiograph shows increased lung markings with fluid in the horizontal fissure. He was delivered by elective caesarean section without labour. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn results from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid and is classically seen after elective caesarean section without labour, with a chest radiograph showing prominent perihilar markings and fluid in the fissures. Respiratory distress syndrome is the closest distractor but occurs in preterm infants and shows a reticulogranular ground-glass pattern with air bronchograms. Meconium aspiration follows meconium-stained liquor, and diaphragmatic hernia shows bowel loops in the chest with mediastinal shift.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has a 4-day history of watery diarrhoea and vomiting. He is lethargic, has sunken eyes, a capillary refill of 4 seconds and no urine output for 10 hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial fluid management?
options: Oral rehydration solution given in small frequent sips
A hypotonic saline bolus of 10 mL/kg
Immediate potassium replacement before any fluid
An isotonic crystalloid bolus of 20 mL/kg given rapidly
questions.explanation: This child has severe dehydration with shock, so the first step is a rapid isotonic crystalloid bolus of 20 mL/kg, repeated as needed, before reassessment. Oral rehydration is appropriate only for mild to moderate dehydration in a child who can drink, and is unsafe in shock. Hypotonic fluid causes rapid shifts and does not restore intravascular volume, and potassium must never be given before adequate urine output is established and circulation restored.

questions.stem: A 10-day-old breastfed baby is brought with poor feeding and lethargy. He was well at discharge. Examination shows a sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes and weight loss of 12 percent from birth weight. Sodium is 158 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Fluid restriction alone without sodium correction
Slow rehydration over 48 hours using an isotonic intravenous fluid
Rapid correction of the sodium with hypertonic saline bolus
questions.explanation: This is hypernatraemic dehydration from inadequate breastfeeding, and the sodium must be lowered slowly over at least 48 hours to avoid cerebral oedema and seizures. Rapid correction with hypertonic or hypotonic boluses risks osmotic demyelination and intracranial haemorrhage. Fluid restriction alone does not restore perfusion, and exchange transfusion has no role in this condition.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is brought after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 8 minutes. He is still convulsing on arrival, has a temperature of 39.5 degrees Celsius, and has no neck stiffness. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.explanation: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is status epilepticus, and a benzodiazepine such as intravenous lorazepam is the first-line agent. Paracetamol treats the fever but does not stop the seizure, and phenytoin is a second-line agent used after benzodiazepines have failed because it acts too slowly for immediate control. Mannitol is used for raised intracranial pressure, which is not evident here.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old infant presents with poor feeding, sweating during feeds and failure to thrive. Examination reveals a bounding precordial impulse, a hyperactive precordium and a harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A large ventricular septal defect presents in the first weeks of life with heart failure, poor feeding, sweating and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge with increased pulmonary blood flow. Tetralogy of Fallot is the closest serious distractor but causes cyanosis and decreased pulmonary vascularity rather than heart failure with plethoric lungs. Atrial septal defect is usually asymptomatic in infancy with a fixed split second sound, and patent ductus arteriosus gives a continuous machinery murmur.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought with a 3-week history of fatigue, and his mother has noticed dark urine. Examination shows periorbital oedema, hypertension and a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and 2+ protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hypertension, oedema, haematuria with red cell casts and a history suggesting recent streptococcal infection points to acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Minimal change disease is the closest distractor but produces heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia without hypertension or red cell casts. IgA nephropathy causes recurrent haematuria with normal complement, and urinary tract infection causes dysuria and pyuria rather than red cell casts.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with a 2-day history of cough, coryza and poor feeding. Examination shows tachypnoea of 60 breaths per minute, subcostal recession, wheeze and fine end-inspiratory crackles. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Bronchiolitis in an infant under 1 year, with coryza, tachypnoea, wheeze and fine crackles, is most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a plausible distractor but typically causes lobar pneumonia with fever and focal consolidation rather than diffuse wheeze. Pertussis produces paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop, and Mycoplasma affects older school-age children.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents with fever of 39 degrees Celsius, cough and pleuritic chest pain. Examination shows tachypnoea and reduced breath sounds at the right base. Chest radiograph shows a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most important initial step in management?
options: Prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics after blood cultures
Simple transfusion to a haemoglobin of 7 g/dL
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease is a medical emergency, and early broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures are essential because infection is a common trigger and is rapidly fatal. Incentive spirometry is an important adjunct but is not a substitute for antibiotics. Simple transfusion is considered for significant hypoxia or anaemia but does not replace antimicrobial therapy, and hydroxyurea is a long-term disease-modifying agent with no role in the acute crisis.

questions.stem: A newborn at 32 weeks gestation develops respiratory distress at 2 hours of life. Chest radiograph shows a diffuse reticulogranular pattern with air bronchograms and low lung volumes. He has not yet received surfactant. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention?
options: Endotracheal surfactant administration with early CPAP support
questions.explanation: The picture is respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant deficiency, and early surfactant replacement together with continuous positive airway pressure reduces mortality and air leak. High-flow nasal cannula alone is the closest reasonable distractor but is insufficient for established RDS with this radiographic severity. Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion, and antibiotics do not correct surfactant deficiency.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old boy presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds and poor weight gain. Examination reveals visible gastric peristaltic waves and an olive-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen. Electrolytes show sodium 132, potassium 3.0, chloride 88 and bicarbonate 32 mmol/L. Which of the following is the correct order of management?
options: Start a proton pump inhibitor and repeat electrolytes in a week
Correct the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, then perform pyloromyotomy
Perform pyloromyotomy immediately before fluid correction
Give oral rehydration and observe for spontaneous resolution
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes vomiting of gastric acid, producing a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria, and surgery must wait until the electrolytes and dehydration are corrected. Operating immediately risks anaesthetic complications from the alkalosis and hypokalaemia. Oral therapy and acid suppression do not relieve the mechanical obstruction and delay definitive care.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with a known ventricular septal defect presents with a 10-day history of fever, malaise and arthralgia. He has a new pansystolic murmur and splinter haemorrhages. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus viridans. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: A single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin
Prolonged intravenous bactericidal antibiotics guided by sensitivities
questions.explanation: This is infective endocarditis on a structural cardiac lesion, and the standard is prolonged intravenous bactericidal therapy, typically 4 to 6 weeks, guided by susceptibility testing. A single dose of benzathine penicillin is prophylaxis for rheumatic fever and does not treat established endocarditis. A short oral course is inadequate for endocardial infection, and surgery is reserved for complications such as valve destruction or persistent infection rather than being a prerequisite for antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is brought with a 6-hour history of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and passage of red currant jelly stool. Examination shows a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant and an empty right iliac fossa. He is irritable between episodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent abdominal ultrasound followed by air or contrast enema reduction
questions.explanation: The presentation is classic for ileocolic intussusception, and ultrasound confirms the target sign before a therapeutic air or contrast enema, which is both diagnostic and curative in most cases. Immediate laparotomy is reserved for peritonitis, perforation or failed enema reduction. A barium meal is contraindicated because it cannot reduce the intussusception and risks perforation, and observation would allow bowel ischaemia to progress.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is admitted with a 2-day history of fever, headache and neck stiffness. He is drowsy and has a petechial rash on the trunk and legs. Lumbar puncture shows a raised neutrophil count with low glucose and high protein. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous fluids and antipyretics only until culture results return
Intravenous ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, with dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose
questions.explanation: The picture is bacterial meningitis, most likely pneumococcal or meningococcal, and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone plus vancomycin covers resistant pneumococcus, with dexamethasone reducing hearing loss and neurological sequelae when given with or just before the first dose. Acyclovir alone would leave bacterial infection untreated and is used for herpes simplex encephalitis. Oral therapy is inadequate for meningitis, and delaying antibiotics until cultures return increases mortality.

questions.stem: A newborn is noted at birth to have cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen. Examination shows a single second heart sound, a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge and no respiratory distress. Chest radiograph shows a boot-shaped heart with diminished pulmonary vascular markings. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate balloon atrial septostomy without prostaglandin
Prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
Supplemental oxygen as the sole therapy
questions.explanation: The findings describe tetralogy of Fallot with duct-dependent pulmonary blood flow, and prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency until surgical repair. Oxygen alone does not improve duct-dependent cyanotic heart disease and may even reduce pulmonary blood flow by relaxing the ductus. Furosemide is used for pulmonary overcirculation rather than reduced pulmonary flow, and balloon atrial septostomy is used for transposition of the great arteries, not tetralogy of Fallot.
